description: Clupai is a one-person team. I'm Sam, and I love building web tools that make big, messy data easy to explore. I'll be on a flight for part of the competition, so I'm going solo this time and not recruiting, but I'm always happy to swap ideas or help out other teams.
summary: NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the whole sky in infrared light, coming back to each part many times. In Slowsky you type a sky position or a star name, or pick one of the challenge's five test targets, and it plays the real SPHEREx frames of that spot one after another, in date order, near one wavelength. Blink makes movement easier to spot. Stack averages the frames so faint things show. Subtract compares two visits you choose. On a live view, False colour makes one picture from two wavelengths, Flagged pixels marks the archive's own quality flags, and Candidate changes lists spots where the light differs between the first and the last visit. Older picture flips to a 2MASS survey picture from 1997 to 2001. Rings from ESA's Gaia catalogue mark the brighter known stars and follow each star's drift. Each frame lists its date, detector, wavelength and original file, and every view is a link you can share. A live view reads only the bytes it needs from NASA's public storage; the test targets open from a small saved copy. A plain-language guide explains the main controls. You need nothing but a browser. Slowsky does not decide what a change is.
details:
Live: https://slowsky.clupai.com · Code (MIT): https://github.com/Clupai8o0/slowsky
Team Clupai, Melbourne. Solo team. Challenge: Planet X and SPHEREx.

The build began on 14 Nov 2026, after kick-off. Before kick-off we only read about the mission and explored the data; none of that work was copied into the product.

What it does

SPHEREx is a NASA space telescope. It maps the whole sky in infrared light (0.75 to 5 µm; the eye stops at about 0.70 µm) in 102 colour channels, and it maps it four times in two years. So each spot has pictures from many dates. A frame is one of those pictures. Slowsky puts the frames of one spot side by side in time.

You can

What the challenge asks for (our paraphrase)

Type RA and Dec (sky coordinates, like longitude and latitude; decimal, or hours-minutes-seconds and degrees) or a star name

Entering the coordinates of a patch of sky

Watch the frames play in date order (Blink), or step through them with buttons, keys or the strip of small dated pictures

Showing a series of images of that patch as a short video

Open Barnard's Star, RW Aurigae, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714 or R Draconis in one click, each with a note on what to look for and what the view cannot tell you

"Test your tool on Barnard's Star"

Average all frames into one picture (Stack) so faint things show

Adding together the data from the detector arrays (partly: one detector and one colour per view)

Pick two visits, A and B, and show B − A or A + B (Subtract)

Adding or subtracting images taken at different times

Choose a field of view of 0.1°, 0.25°, 0.5° or 1°

Letting users choose the field of view

Turn on rings for the brighter stars in ESA's Gaia DR3 catalogue, moved to each frame's date (Blink and Stack)

Overlaying data from other telescopes, such as Gaia

Copy a link that reopens the exact view: position, field, colour, frame and mode

Opening the tool with coordinates in the URL

Read each frame's date, wavelength, detector, data release and file name, with links to the original file

Showing metadata such as contamination flags

On a live view in Blink, switch on Flagged pixels to paint the pixels the frame's own quality layer marks, such as cosmic-ray hits, and read how many are flagged and the three most common kinds

same as above

Pick a wavelength from 0.75 to 5.00 µm with a slider, which also picks one of SPHEREx's six detectors

A creative way to show the 102 infrared bands

On a live view in Stack, switch on False colour: one picture from the wavelength on screen and a partner (4.60 µm when the one on screen is below 2.42 µm, otherwise 1.25 µm). Blue means brighter at the shorter wavelength, orange brighter at the longer one

same as above

In Blink on the 0.1° or 0.25° field, switch on Older picture to flip between the SPHEREx frame and the 2MASS K survey picture, taken between June 1997 and February 2001. On the 0.25° field a bracket marks where Barnard's Star's catalogue motion puts it in those years

Overlaying data from other telescopes

On a live view, read Candidate changes: a list of spots where the light differs between the first and the last visit, each marked on the sky with a numbered ring

Making it easy to see how the sky changes over time and to spot what moved

In the inspector's Charts tab, press Read the spectrum here in the Spectrum card: the page reads the light at the centre of the view in SPHEREx's 102 colours from the archive's all-sky cube and draws a small chart. Nothing is read before the press. It is a quick look, not a measurement

A creative way to show the 102 infrared bands

Read the Tonight's sky line in the inspector's Target tab: when the spot on screen stands highest in tonight's dark hours as seen from Melbourne, about how high, and facing which way. It says where the spot is in the sky, never whether anything can be seen there

Our own addition, not asked for

In Subtract, press Save picture (the download button in the top bar): one PNG, drawn in the browser, with the earlier visit, the later visit and their difference side by side, the data credit, a line saying the code was written with AI tools and a line saying a difference is a candidate only. The page itself sends the picture nowhere

Adding or subtracting images taken at different times

Look at the Comet 3I/ATLAS across the CO₂ band card in the inspector's Extras tab: twelve small pictures of the interstellar comet from SPHEREx frames taken on 14 Dec 2025, and a chart of its core's brightness by wavelength. The numbers are raw image values with rough sums of our own, not a calibrated measurement of the comet

A creative way to show the infrared bands

Press My frames (or drop files on the page) to try 2 to 20 of your own FITS, PNG or JPG pictures of one patch of sky: the page lines them up and shows them in Blink, Stack and Subtract, with a list of candidate changes between two picked frames. It all runs in the browser and the files are never uploaded. For PNG and JPG pictures the σ beside a candidate is marked rough (≈): it is for choosing where to look, not a measurement. Try real FITS samples runs three SPHEREx cutouts of Groombridge 1830 through the same steps

Our own addition, not asked for

On a touchscreen, swipe on the sky picture to step through frames, and in Blink press and hold on a later frame to see the first frame until you let go. The gestures pause while the page is pinch-zoomed

Showing a series of images of that patch as a short video

Look at the Planet Nine: how faint, how deep? chart under the comet card: published estimates of how bright Planet Nine would be and one example from this repo's own model, beside how deep SPHEREx and three optical searches reach. The rows are in different bands, so it is a rough comparison, not a search result

Planet X: how faint it would be, beside how deep the surveys reach

New to astronomy? Press What am I looking at? ("Help" on a phone or a narrow laptop) for a plain-language guide: one line on each of the main controls and a short list of the words the page uses. A second Help button at the foot of the page opens the same guide. Short notes on the page explain µm, Gaia and 2MASS, and the Candidate changes list explains S/N, catalogue star and the ″ (arcsecond) mark when they appear

A public-facing tool that makes it easy for anyone to see how the sky changes

It also draws a rough brightness curve for RW Aurigae. WISE 0855 gets one only on a live view whose field holds at least two suitable comparison stars; its saved copy has too few. The other three presets never get one. On a phone, the page becomes one column you can add to your home screen.

Spectrum. In the inspector's Charts tab, a button reads the light at the centre of the view in SPHEREx's 102 colours and draws a small chart. It reads the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky cube (doi:10.26131/IRSA679) from the same public archive, and nothing is read before the press. In our six reads on 15 Nov 2026 a read took 34 to 36 seconds and about 2.1 MB. The chart is a quick look, not a measurement: the colours of one spot were not all observed at the same time, a neighbour inside the same 12.9 arcsec pixels can change what is read, some colours can be blank (Barnard's Star had data in 9 of 102 in our read), and stripes from Earth's airglow can sit near 1.083 µm. The labels mark where known features fall, not that a feature is there.

AI note. In the inspector's AI note tab, the Write an AI note button asks Claude Opus 5.5, through the Claude API, to write a short reading of the view from the numbers the page itself measured. Its heading reads "AI-generated" followed by the model's name ("AI-generated: Claude Opus 5.5"), and the page says it can be wrong. Before you see it, a checker keeps only sentences that match a fixed list of sentence forms, filled in with the words and numbers of the fact sheet built from the page's own measurements, and drops every other sentence. It is a filter, not a proof: it checks the note against the fact sheet, not the measurements themselves. The note is open to every visitor, with no passcode: up to 15 new notes a day per network address, and hourly and daily limits for the whole site.

How it works

  1. Position. You give a sky position. For the five presets, Slowsky stores each target's catalogue position and proper motion (the slow drift of a star or brown dwarf across the sky, year by year).
  2. Frame lookup. A small server function asks NASA's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) which SPHEREx frames cover the spot. The function exists because IRSA's search does not accept calls from other websites' pages. It lets through only the DR1 and QR3 releases.
  3. Only the needed bytes. The frames are FITS files (the standard astronomy image format) in NASA's public Amazon S3 bucket. The browser reads each file's header, its wavelength table and only the part that covers the view, from the image and from the layers stored with it (the zodiacal-light model; the quality layer when Flagged pixels is on; and, for Candidate changes, the quality layer and the error map). It never downloads a whole file.
  4. Same wavelength. In a SPHEREx frame, each part of the detector sees a slightly different wavelength (colour of light). Slowsky groups one detector's frames into visits: a visit takes in every frame that starts up to 10 days after its first one. For each visit, it keeps the one frame whose wavelength at the spot is closest to your choice, and only if your choice falls within half that spot's bandwidth. It leaves out other visits and says how many. Near a strong spectral line even that small difference can matter. (Subtract groups the frames on show a little differently: each taken less than 10 days after the one before.)
  5. Moving targets. For a preset, Slowsky moves the target by its proper motion to each frame's own date.
  6. Lining up. It removes zodiacal light (the glow of sunlit dust in the solar system), using the archive's own model in each file. Then it puts every frame on one north-up grid, using the sky mapping in each file's header.
  7. Drawing. All frames and the Stack picture share one brightness scale, so a frame that looks brighter has higher values in the data (after the zodiacal light is removed). Higher values are not always a real change in the sky; see Limits.
  8. Saved copy first. The five presets open at once from a small saved copy of real SPHEREx frames that ships with the site (24 frames per target). Go live reads the same target fresh from the archive. If the archive does not answer, a preset falls back to the saved copy. The status line says which one you see.
  9. Older picture. When you switch it on, the page reads IRSA's copy of the 2MASS K image tiles. No 2MASS pixels are stored with the site.
  10. Candidate changes. On a live view, the page compares the first and the last visit, and only when their wavelengths differ by no more than 0.02 µm. SPHEREx's wavelength changes across each frame, so two visits that match at the centre can differ away from it: wherever the average wavelengths of the two visits' frames differ by more than 0.02 µm, that part of the picture is left out, and a note gives the share left out. It reads the archive's error map for each frame of the two visits, to judge how far a spot stands out from the noise. It leaves out a spot when, in a frame of a checked visit, the brightest of up to four detector pixels at or beside the brightest point within 12 arcseconds of it carries one of the archive's TRANSIENT, OUTLIER, NONFUNC or SUR_ERROR flags (quality marks the archive sets on a pixel, for example for a cosmic-ray hit), and it says how many it left out. The list opens with at most 8 spots that have no star in the loaded Gaia star list within 6 arcseconds (a tiny angle); the rest stay behind a button, because a small shift between two pictures of a star can look like a change. The loaded Gaia star list holds at most the 400 brightest stars, and on the 0.5° and 1° fields it covers only a circle of radius 0.2° around the centre, so a spot with no listed star within 6 arcseconds that lies outside that circle, or within 6 arcseconds of its edge, is marked as not checked against the list and comes last; a note says when the star list was cut short. A saved copy lists nothing, because it is not checked against the error maps and flags.

Who it helps

  • People with no astronomy background. The guide gives one line on each of the main controls and a short list of the words the page uses, in plain language.
  • Volunteers and amateur astronomers. The challenge page says volunteers comparing sky images found most of the known comets and brown dwarfs. Slowsky gives them SPHEREx frames for any spot without software to install.
  • Teachers and students. The five presets each say what to look for and what the picture cannot show. A class can open the same view from one link.
  • Anyone checking a result. Every frame links to its original file and the archive's own page, so you can go back to the source.

What is new

What Slowsky adds to a plain blink viewer:

  • Colour-matched frames. A SPHEREx frame sees each spot at one wavelength. Slowsky picks one frame per visit at matched wavelength, so a colour difference is less likely to pass for a brightness change.
  • Reading the archive in place. The browser reads small pieces of NASA's own files from S3. No copy of the archive sits on our server.
  • Honest target cards. Each preset card has a "What this can't tell you" line beside "What to look for".
  • Gaia rings that move. Each ring sits where that star should be on that frame's date, from its catalogue motion.
  • Works when the archive is slow. The saved copy of the five presets keeps the demo working if IRSA is down.
  • Two colours in one picture. False colour shows where a spot is brighter at the shorter or the longer wavelength, and lists its own limits under the picture.
  • Then and now for Barnard's Star. Older picture flips to a 2MASS picture from 1997 to 2001. On the 0.25° field the star sits away from its ring there, and a bracket marks where its catalogue motion puts it in those years.
  • A change list that screens itself. Candidate changes leaves out spots with certain archive flags, such as TRANSIENT (cosmic-ray hits), and puts spots next to known Gaia stars behind a button. It says above the list that every line is a candidate only.
  • A guide for newcomers. "What am I looking at?" explains each control and the page's words in plain language. Each fact in it is listed with its source in SOURCES.md, under "Help text".

Choice

Why

One wavelength and one detector per view

Frames at different colours would look like a change in brightness

One brightness scale for all frames

A brighter frame then means higher values in the data

North up on one grid

Most stars stay put from frame to frame, so one that moves stands out

The word "candidate" for anything that stands out

A change can be noise, a satellite trail or a camera artefact

Flags never change the pictures, the brightness curve or the motion check; only the Candidate changes list uses them

The list leaves out spots with certain flags and cautions others. Everywhere else you see the archive's own quality marks and judge them yourself

False colour and Older picture are pictures for looking, not measurements

False colour's two wavelengths were not taken at the same times. The older picture is from another telescope at another wavelength, so its brightness cannot be compared with SPHEREx

Saved copy first for the presets

A live read takes time (our rough timing: 20 to 45 seconds)

Plain words, with a guide and short notes for the terms

The page is for people with no astronomy background

A link for every view

You can send a class or a friend the exact picture you saw

How we checked it

Tests run with npm test. Three are gates that every change must pass:

Gate

What it checks

Pass mark

WCS (sky mapping)

Slowsky's pixel-to-sky mapping against astropy, at 9 points on each of two real frames, both directions

within 0.01 pixel

S3 cutout

A box of pixels read from S3, summed, against astropy's value. This one needs the network, so it runs with LIVE=1 npm test; plain npm test checks that a reply that is not a partial read is refused

within 1 part in 1,000

Regrid

Simulated field stars across epochs, against each other and their true position

within 0.3 pixel

  • Other tests cover the archive proxy, the saved copy, coordinate input, the player, stacking and the link format.
  • A browser test (npm run smoke) opens the five presets in headless Chromium with the archive blocked.
  • Barnard's Star. The page measures how far the star moved between two frames and shows the shift its catalogue proper motion predicts beside it. The two can differ: the prediction leaves out parallax (the small yearly shift from Earth's orbit), and the star's bright core is hard to centre.
  • Older picture facts. Its dates (June 1997 to February 2001) and its wavelength band come from the 2MASS tile set's own description file at IRSA, read on 14 Nov 2026.
  • Facts on the page. SOURCES.md lists every fact in the README, the page and the target cards with its source. Claude opened the sources it could reach and matched the claims. Gemini, a model from another maker, then read the claims and the list as text and marked anything it judged wrong. Codex and Grok each rechecked part of the list against its sources. AI tools ran these checks; no person has yet gone through the list line by line.

Limits

  • Slowsky shows changes between frames. It does not decide what a change is. Anything that stands out is a candidate for a closer look.
  • It is not a planet finder. Optical surveys (ZTF, DES and Pan-STARRS1) have together ruled out about 78% of Planet Nine's predicted range, and what is left is faint, around V magnitude 22 (Brown, Holman & Batygin 2024). SPHEREx reaches 19.5 to 19.9 AB magnitude (5 sigma) below 3.8 µm, and 17.8 to 18.8 from 3.8 to 5 µm, only after its two-year survey, with four observations in each channel at a typical sky brightness away from the Milky Way's plane (Bock et al. 2025). One frame is shallower still; that part is our own reasoning, not a number from the paper. These are different bands, so this is a rough comparison.
  • A live view reads at most 60 frames and says so. It picks them by estimating each frame's wavelength at the spot from the archive's list (about 10 pixels off), or spreads them evenly in time when it cannot. At very busy spots, such as near the ecliptic poles, the archive can cut its frame list short, and the page says so.
  • Gaia rings mark only stars brighter than G magnitude 19, and at most the 40 brightest in each picture. A live view fetches Gaia stars only within 0.2° of the centre, and the saved copy holds those within 0.1°, so the outer part of a wide field has no rings. Blink and Stack show them; Subtract does not. A live view skips them if the catalogue is slow to answer.
  • Gaia rings start from the catalogue's 2016.0 positions, so a fast star that walked into the field since then has no ring.
  • The target marker moves with proper motion only for the five presets. A star found by name stays at its catalogue position.
  • The brightness curve divides the target by two to four Gaia comparison stars of G magnitude 9 to 15 (a range we chose). They are barely checked for steadiness, so a variable one shows as wobble. It is a rough check, not calibrated photometry.
  • Stack and Subtract use plain averages, so a cosmic-ray hit in one frame still shows, only fainter.
  • False colour is a picture for looking, not a measurement. Its two wavelengths were not taken at the same times, and areas where not every frame has usable pixels are hatched instead of coloured. The page lists these limits under the picture.
  • The older picture is also for looking, not measuring. It comes from a different telescope at a different wavelength (2.16 µm), its brightness cannot be compared with SPHEREx, and the night it was taken is not known. On the 0.1° field Barnard's Star's older spot is outside the view, and the page says so.
  • Flagged pixels leaves out three kinds of flag (SOURCE, FULLSAMPLE and GHOST_FPA). A flagged pixel beside a very bright star can be spilled charge and not a cosmic ray, and hits in the first ten seconds of an exposure may go unflagged.
  • Candidate changes compares only the first and the last visit, at one wavelength, and it cannot confirm any spot it lists. It cannot tell a real change in the sky from a detector hit, a sharper star image in one visit or a small shift between the two pictures, and it says so above the list. When a visit has fewer than 3 frames, the page cannot rule out a detector hit, and it says so. The Gaia star list holds at most the 400 brightest stars in a circle around the centre (at most 0.2° in radius). So on a wide field a spot with no listed star within 6 arcseconds that lies outside that circle, or within 6 arcseconds of its edge, is marked as not checked against it, and a faint catalogue star can be missing from the list; a note says when the star list was cut short.
  • The change list's flag check has limits too. An OVERFLOW flag near a spot does not remove it: the line says the reading there can be unreliable, and no longer says which visit is brighter. The TRANSIENT flag can miss hits in the first ten seconds of an exposure, so an unflagged spot is not proof of a clean one.
  • The centre of R Draconis is too bright for the camera in all 24 saved frames, and Barnard's Star's in 22 of 24. The camera stores no value there.
  • The saved copy holds only the five presets, one detector each, at most 0.1° across.

Experimental parts, switched on 15 Nov

Three parts were held back until the last day and are now on. Each is labelled on the page for what it is.

  • Colour reading. With False colour on, a live view gives one sentence on the spot at the centre: whether light is seen at each of the two wavelengths and, where it is seen, how far above the noise it is. The 0.5° and 1° fields give no reading and say why. It is a rough reading of the picture, not a colour measurement.
  • R Draconis halo. The star's centre is too bright for the camera, so the Charts tab measures the light in a ring around the blank centre on each usable look, against nearby Gaia stars, with an error bar on each reading. It draws a line only when at least three visits match closely in colour; otherwise it lists each reading in a table.
  • Sort hint (machine learning). On a live view, each candidate change gets one line from a small neural network trained only on fake changes added to real frames. The squares the page hands it are not the kind it learned from, and two AI reviews (Gemini and Claude Opus) advised against switching it on; we show it anyway, labelled on the page "Experimental sort hint, trained only on fake changes added to single frames. Never tested on real two-date changes. Not a verdict." It can give no label (7 of 17 candidates on Barnard's Star in our check on 15 Nov 2026), and it never reorders, adds or removes candidates.

Every sky picture on the site is real telescope data: SPHEREx pixels, and 2MASS pixels in Older picture. In the film, the sky shown as data is real SPHEREx pixels; the AI images and a drawn starfield are backdrops and decoration, never data.

The demo film shows one line on screen: "AI images: OpenAI gpt-image-2 · AI voice: ElevenLabs eleven_multilingual_v2". Its end credits repeat both. The sound effects and the music bed are synthesised in code (numpy), not recorded and not made by an AI audio model; the code was written with Claude Opus 5.5. Each AI-made item, with the model that made it and where the record of the request is kept, is listed in SOURCES.md under "AI-generated content". The guide on the page ends with a line that says the code, the wording and the icon were made with AI tools, and links to that list.
